ety.text: Inherited from Middle English tyde, from Old English tīd, from Proto-West Germanic *tīdi, from Proto-Germanic *tīdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₂itis, from *deh₂y- + *-tis. Related to time. Cognate with Dutch tijd (“time”), German Zeit (“time”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish tid (“time”), Faroese and Icelandic tíð (“time”).
From Middle English tiden, tide, from Old English tīdan (“to happen”).

senses.d: The daily fluctuation in the level of the sea caused by the gravitational influence of the moon and the sun.
ex: The Bristol Channel has some of the world's largest tides.

senses.d: The associated flow of water.
ex: A lot of driftwood was brought in on the tide.
We can cross to the island when the tide is out, but it won't move out until around five o'clock.

senses.d: Any similar gravitational effect on Earth or other body.
ex: As well as sea tides, there are much smaller land tides.
By far the largest tides on Europa are those caused by the gravitational attraction of Jupiter.

senses.d: A high-volume flow, literal or figurative; a current or flood.
ex: The sewer burst, and a tide of sewage poured into nearby properties.
A tide of people crossed over the border.

senses.d: The tendency or direction of causes, influences, or events; course; current.
ex: The tide of public opinion has turned.
There is a tide in the affairs of men, / Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune […]

senses.d: Time, notably anniversary, period or season linked to an ecclesiastical feast.
ex: [...] and rest their weary limbs a tide.
Which, at th'appointed tyde, / Each one did make his Bryde

senses.d: A time.
ex: The doctor's no good this tide.

senses.d: A point or period of time identified or described by a qualifier.
ex: Eventide, noontide, morrowtide, nighttide, moontide, harvesttide, wintertide, summertide, springtide, autumntide etc.

senses.d: The period of twelve hours.
To cause to float with the tide; to drive or carry with the tide or stream.
ex: They are tided down the stream.

senses.d: To carry over or through a problem or difficulty.
To pour a tide or flood.
ex: The ocean tided most impressively.

senses.d: To work into or out of a river or harbor by drifting with the tide and anchoring when it becomes adverse.
To happen, occur.
ex: I wit not what may tide us here

grp.label: periodic change of sea level — see also flood tide, ebb tide, high tide, low tide
tendency or direction of causes, influences or events; course; current

it:corso.gl: course (of a river, of a university, etc.)

phr: a rising tide lifts all boats

ety.text: Latin -ālisbor. Old French -albor. ▲ Latin -ālis Old French -elbor. ▲ Latin -ālisbor. Middle English -al English -al English tidal From tide + -al. Probably a hybrid formation within English. Alternatively it might be from an unattested British Medieval Latin *tīdālis, derived from rare tīda, from Old English tīd. The usual Latin word for “tidal” is aestuālis.

senses.d: Relating to tides.

ety.text: From Middle English tidy, tydy, tidi (“timely, seasonal, opportune”), from tide (“time”) + -y. Cognate with Saterland Frisian tiedig (“timely, early”), Dutch tijdig (“timely”), German Low German tiedig (“timely”), German zeitig (“seasonal, timely”), Danish tidig (“timely”), Swedish tidig (“timely”).

senses.d: Arranged neatly and in order.
ex: She always kept her desk immaculately tidy; nothing was ever out of place.

senses.d: Not messy; neat and controlled.
ex: Keep Britain tidy by picking up litter.

senses.d: Satisfactory; comfortable.
Generous, considerable.
ex: The scheme made a tidy profit.
Two hundred thousand people! Miss Glory, that's a tidy lot. Not bad.

senses.d: In good time; at the right time; timely; seasonable; opportune; favourable; fit; suitable.
ex: if weather be fair and tidy

senses.d: Brave; smart; skillful; fine; good.
Appropriate or suitable as regards occasion, circumstances, arrangement, or order.
Normalized in a certain way that optimizes for data analysis.
To make tidy; to neaten.
A container or other device for storing or organizing loose items in a tidy fashion.
ex: desk tidy; sink tidy; cable tidy
It was in the days when[…]every scrap of cotton or linen found its way into the ‘tidy’.

senses.d: A cover, often of tatting, drawn work, or other ornamental work, for the back of a chair, the arms of a sofa, etc.
A child's pinafore.
The wren.
ex: The Tydie for her notes as delicate as they

senses.d: Expression of agreement or positive acknowledgement, usually in reply to a question; great, fine.

ety.text: From Old French net, inherited from Latin nitidus (“shiny”) through a contracted Vulgar Latin form *nittus. Doublet of nitide, a borrowing.
From Latin polītus. Cf. the doublet polito.
From Latin pulchrum, accusative form of pulcher.
Borrowed from Latin prōlixus (“courteous, favorable”). Compare Catalan prolix, Portuguese prolixo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese limpo, limpio, from Latin limpidus. Compare límpido, a borrowed doublet.

chain.g: to arrange, put in order, organize
